hypothesis.title: Accounting consumer intrinsically slow (~480ms/msg), causing lag spike to 2,238
hypothesis.summary: The accounting Kafka consumer began processing messages very slowly (~480ms each, up from ~30ms) around 10 minutes before the alert, with no corresponding slowdown in its postgresql dependency (p95 stable at 4ms). Accounting's own spans account for 100% of the added latency. With CPU and memory utilization normal and no recent deploy or config change to accounting, the consumer is intrinsically too slow per message, causing lag to grow from 12 to over 2,200 messages.
hypothesis.reasoning: The alert fired on accounting consumer lag exceeding 1000 messages. The evidence shows accounting's p95 latency jumped from ~36ms to 491ms starting around -10m, and consumer lag grew from ~12 to 2,238 messages in the same window. The slow trace shows accounting's own span (accounting/handle) taking 424ms, and logs confirm "Consumer poll interval exceeded; processing 1 message took 480ms." This indicates accounting itself is slow, not just propagating errors. I need to determine why accounting became slow. Accounting calls postgresql, so I checked postgresql's metrics: p95 latency is stable at ~4ms, CPU ~12%, memory ~45%, request rate steady, error rate flat at 0.4%. PostgreSQL is healthy. Accounting's own CPU is 11% and memory 40%, so it is not saturated or leaking. The frontend-proxy deploy at -25m is a red herring: it happened 15 minutes before accounting's latency spike at -10m, and frontend-proxy does not call accounting (kafka does). The valkey-cart restart (exit 137, OOMKilled) is also unrelated—accounting does not depend on valkey-cart. Postmortem PM-2026-06-17 describes a similar pattern (accounting lag from slow Postgres), but here Postgres is demonstrably healthy. With no deploy, config change, or dependency issue, and accounting's own spans being slow while its CPU/memory are fine, the most likely mechanism is that accounting's message-processing logic has become intrinsically slow—possibly due to a data pattern or an unobserved internal bottleneck. This fits the queue_backlog category: the consumer is too slow per message, dependencies are healthy, and no other specific mechanism (CPU, memory, crash) applies.

supporting_evidence.why_it_matters: Shows a single accounting span (accounting/handle) taking 424ms, confirming the slowness originates in accounting's own processing, not a downstream call.
300 log entries stating 'processing 1 message took 480ms' directly confirm the per-message slowdown in the consumer.
PostgreSQL p95 latency is stable at ~4ms throughout the incident, ruling out datastore degradation as the cause.
Accounting CPU remains around 11%, ruling out CPU saturation as the mechanism.
Memory is flat at ~40%, ruling out memory leak or GC pressure.
Frontend-proxy deploy at -25m is 15 minutes before the spike and frontend-proxy does not call accounting, so this is a red herring.

suggested_actions.title: Inspect accounting logs and recent messages for anomalous data patterns
suggested_actions.rationale: The slowdown may be triggered by a specific message shape or data pattern (e.g., large payloads, complex transactions). Check logs around -15m to -10m for unusual entries or stack traces.

suggested_actions.title: Scale accounting consumer replicas to increase throughput and drain the lag
suggested_actions.rationale: Even if the per-message slowness persists, adding replicas will increase aggregate throughput and prevent lag from growing further while you investigate the root cause.

suggested_actions.title: Restart accounting pods to clear any transient internal state
suggested_actions.rationale: If an in-memory cache, connection, or internal queue is stuck, a restart may restore normal processing speed. However, this is speculative and may only provide temporary relief.

alternatives.why_less_likely: PostgreSQL's own p95 latency is stable at 4ms, CPU at 12%, and error rate flat. Postmortem PM-2026-06-17 had a similar symptom but Postgres was demonstrably slow there; here it is healthy.

retrieved_documents.title: Cart / Valkey errors and timeouts
retrieved_documents.snippet: Decide whether the problem is the client pool or the server. - Server: `kubectl -n otel-demo exec deploy/valkey-cart -- valkey-cli --latency` and `SLOWLOG GET 10`. High latency or `BUSY` => datastore degradation. - Client: server latency flat but cart logs `pool busy=N/N` or "timeout awaiting connection" => pool exhaustion. Raise the pool size and restart cart.
